jeffrey/lbs · LBS = lift + Bellman + segment · rectangle robot in SE(2), ntrl-demo’s MPPI, exact scoring · every number from registered runs

LBS Bellman benchmarking: lift + Bellman + segment, with each part removed in turn

LBS adds three things to ntrl-demo: the travel-time lift of the input, a Bellman backup over short collision-free steps priced by the true speed, and the travel-time midpoint (segment) loss on paths the planner drives. Every scene is trained five ways: ntrl-demo, LBS, and LBS with one part removed. One training seed (87358) per arm so far. Mazes (10 × 10, 13 × 13, 18 × 18): LBS 100.0 / 99.5 / 94.6 % of the queries solved, ntrl-demo 83.3 / 64.2 / 35.4 %, no lift 92.0 / 69.2 / 49.4 %, no Bellman 94.3 / 88.7 / 46.9 %, no segment 94.5 / 98.3 / 86.5 %. 10 × 10 gap mazes (gap ×1, gap ×2, gap ×4): LBS 100.0 / 99.9 / 99.3 % of the queries solved, ntrl-demo 70.2 / 45.8 / 33.0 %, no lift 81.8 / 78.9 / 63.9 %, no Bellman 71.0 / 41.6 / 27.0 %, no segment 100.0 / 99.8 / 94.1 %. Gibson houses (Allensville, Lakeville): LBS 93.4 / 90.8 % of the queries solved, ntrl-demo 83.9 / 72.7 %, no lift 98.8 / 44.9 %, no Bellman 84.6 / 60.7 %, no segment 95.0 / 97.0 %.

40 of 40 scene × arm results are in.

Gibson houses in 3-D: a point robot in R³

Asked on 2026-11-20: the first 3-D test. Five Gibson houses (Allensville and Lakeville from the 2-D set, plus Mifflinburg, Noxapater and Markleeville), LBS against ntrl-demo only. The robot is a point that flies: its configuration is (x, y, z). Each house is the scan’s mesh at 2.5 cm voxels inside a slab of the main floor, 0.15 to 2.15 m above the floor (one cell is 0.25 m as in the 2-D houses, so the slab is 8 cells high). Every voxel that holds a piece of the mesh is an obstacle, and so is the outside of the house and everything below and above the slab; free space is the connected air of the rooms, so a path can go over or under furniture and has to go through the doors.

The lift is onto four dimensions: the network’s input is (x, y, z, h), with h the travel-time height of the point computed from its clearance, exactly the lift of the 2-D tests, whose input is (x, y, heading, h). The rule in both is input dimensions + 1. Bellman and segment are unchanged. Planner, scorer, training length and seed are those of the 2-D houses.

10 of 10 runs are in; 5 of 5 houses are prepared (voxels, training pairs, ground truth, test queries).

Seen from above: how much of the 2 m slab above each spot is free air (white = all of it, dark = none; furniture shows as grey). Blue: the true path of the longest test query, from its start (dot) to its goal (ring), flattened onto the plan. The robot is a point.

  • LBS minus ntrl-demo, points of queries solved: Allensville 3−D +13.6, Mifflinburg 3−D +22.4, Noxapater 3−D +19.9, Markleeville 3−D +13.2, Lakeville 3−D +9.8.
  • How the failures split (through a wall / stalled, % of runs): Allensville 3-D: ntrl-demo 35.3 / 0.0, LBS 0.1 / 21.5; Mifflinburg 3-D: ntrl-demo 28.9 / 2.9, LBS 0.0 / 9.4; Noxapater 3-D: ntrl-demo 18.2 / 6.2, LBS 0.0 / 4.6; Markleeville 3-D: ntrl-demo 17.6 / 3.1, LBS 0.0 / 7.5; Lakeville 3-D: ntrl-demo 41.8 / 0.0, LBS 0.2 / 31.8.
  • Controls on the same queries: a straight line solves Allensville 3-D 55.8 %, Mifflinburg 3-D 52.1 %, Noxapater 3-D 58.3 %, Markleeville 3-D 64.6 %, Lakeville 3-D 53.6 %; the same planner driven by the true travel time solves Allensville 3-D 96.2 %, Mifflinburg 3-D 98.5 %, Noxapater 3-D 98.8 %, Markleeville 3-D 97.9 %, Lakeville 3-D 93.3 %.
  • Reading: LBS is ahead of ntrl-demo on all 5 houses, by 9.8 to 22.4 points (average 69.2 % → 85.0 %). ntrl-demo fails by arriving through walls; LBS almost never does and fails by stalling, mostly on the long queries: of the 32–64 cell queries it solves Allensville 3-D 28 %, Mifflinburg 3-D 70 %, Noxapater 3-D 88 %, Markleeville 3-D 62 %, Lakeville 3-D 23 % (ntrl-demo 18 %, 28 %, 21 %, 25 %, 10 %). The planner on the true travel time solves 93 to 99 %, so the queries themselves are solvable; why LBS stalls more on Allensville and Lakeville than on the other three is not tested.
  • One training seed per arm.

Ground truth: shortest travel time on a grid with 5 nodes per cell in all three directions, every grid edge that touches an obstacle removed (the scans’ walls are as thin as one voxel, 0.1 cells). Queries: 40 per true-distance bin, each certified by a collision-free true path. jeffrey/lbs/scenes3.py, prepare3.py.

A cut-off part on Lakeville. The scene’s free space is one connected piece at the 2.5 cm voxels, but on Lakeville the truth grid does not connect about 4 % of it to the rest (an opening too narrow for the grid’s edges, which are 5 cm long and are removed when they touch a wall). Three of the 48 truth goals and 4 of the 280 test queries lie inside that part; no test query crosses into it. The other four houses have no such part larger than 0.2 % of the pairs.

What the results show

  • LBS solves 90.8 to 100.0 % of the queries on the 8 scenes finished so far; ntrl-demo 33.0 to 83.9 %. LBS is ahead of ntrl-demo on every one of them, by 9.5 to 66.3 points.
  • Lift is worth 8.0 to 45.1 points on the mazes and gap mazes (10 × 10 +8.0, 13 × 13 +30.3, 18 × 18 +45.1, gap ×1 +18.2, gap ×2 +21.0, gap ×4 +35.4). Without it the failures are plans through a wall: 7.5 to 44.6 % of the runs, against 0.0 to 0.6 % for LBS. On the houses it is needed on the larger one (Lakeville +46.0) and not on the smallest (Allensville −5.3). Without lift the larger house fails by stalling (54.6 % of the runs), not through walls, and ends below ntrl-demo: the travel times stop growing beyond about 8 to 16 cells (the lift section).
  • Bellman is worth 5.7 to 72.3 points (10 × 10 +5.7, 13 × 13 +10.8, 18 × 18 +47.6, gap ×1 +29.0, gap ×2 +58.3, gap ×4 +72.3, Allensville +8.8, Lakeville +30.1). Without it the failures are stalls: 5.7 to 73.0 % of the runs, against 0.0 to 9.2 % for LBS. Within the regular mazes and within the gap mazes, both parts are worth more as the scene grows.
  • Segment is the smallest of the three and not always a gain: 10 × 10 +5.5, 13 × 13 +1.2, 18 × 18 +8.1, gap ×1 +0.0, gap ×2 +0.1, gap ×4 +5.2, Allensville −1.6, Lakeville −6.2 points (LBS minus no segment, both trained here). It helps on the regular mazes and the widest gap maze and has nothing left to add where the arm without it already solves everything. On the houses: Allensville −1.6, Lakeville −6.2; see the house section.
  • One training seed per arm (two on Allensville for LBS and no segment). Differences of a few points between arms are within what a second seed can move.

Segment variants inside LBS

Asked on 2026-11-20: put two variants of the travel-time midpoint loss in as the segment part of LBS, without ablations. Safe, min leaves, tree + sub-paths is that page’s main setting and is what every LBS run here already uses, so the LBS results are that test. Plain, min leaves, tree changes two things: the training drives are the test planner’s own (nothing keeps a rollout 0.02 cells off the walls; a drive that touches a wall is cut there), and the loss uses only the pieces of the midpoint tree, without the random sub-paths between leaf ends. Lift, Bellman, training seed and GPU are those of the scene’s LBS run, so the pair is the same run up to epoch 2,000. The run without the segment loss is shown as the reference.

The method and the five arms

LBSLift + Bellman + segment: everything.
no liftBellman + segment on ntrl-demo’s own input.
no BellmanLift + segment; no backup.
no segmentLift + Bellman; no midpoint loss.
ntrl-demoThe original baseline: none of the three.

L, lift. The network gets one more input column, the travel-time height of the configuration, h(q) = G(d(q)) / E with G(d) the integral of √(1 / S² − 1) from the clearance d to the speed margin (jeffrey/lift_scale; no push, no octaves, gain 1).

B, Bellman. For each end q of a training pair (q, g): y = min over 16 straight steps q → q′ that stay out of obstacles of [τ(q, q′) + T(q′, g)], loss (T(q, g) − y)², from epoch 1. As asked, the backup uses the ground truth: τ is the step’s travel time at the true speed (its lifted length) and the steps are checked against the true geometry. Steps of 0.33–0.66 cells; on scenes larger than 24 cells (gap ×4 and the houses) lengths up to 5.3 cells. ntrl-demo’s own TD term skips steps that cross an obstacle (jeffrey/pair_lift’s recipe).

S, segment. The travel-time midpoint loss of the midpoint page, its main setting: from epoch 2,000, every 100 epochs the current field drives 8,192 random pairs with ntrl-demo’s MPPI; each drive is split recursively at travel-time midpoints down to one-cell leaves, and the network’s time over a piece is pulled to the sum over its leaves (|log T − log target|, weight ramped over 500 epochs).

All arms: ntrl-demo’s network, loss, data (500,000 pairs) and 5,000 epochs; the rectangle robot (0.5 × 0.2 cells) in SE(2); the scene’s certified test queries, ntrl-demo’s MPPI with planning seeds 0, 1 and 2, a run solved when it reaches the goal without touching an obstacle.

The houses: does the segment loss hurt?

Allensville

The first LBS run on Allensville solved 92.5 %, below the 100.0 % of the no-segment run reused from the pair-lift study. Asked to make sure the segment loss is really harmful there, I re-ran the no-segment arm with this benchmark’s code, the same training seed and the same GPU as the LBS run: 94.2 %. The two runs are identical through epoch 2,000, where the segment loss starts.

  • The gap to 100 % is not the segment loss. Without segment, the same code and seed give 94.2 %; with it 92.5 %. The difference is 4 of 240 queries; 14 failed queries are the same in both.
  • It is one room. 23 of the 240 queries start in the room at the top left of the house (15 of the 40 longest). 14 of the 14 failures without segment and 15 of the 18 with it start there, on every planning seed. In each run the plans stop at one spot just outside it, (-9.7, 9.0) cells without segment and (-8.3, 7.9) with it: the field has a local minimum on the way out of that room.
  • The room opens and closes during training, in every run. Both runs of this benchmark solve 236 of 240 at epoch 4,000 and fall back at 5,000. The earlier study’s run failed on the same room at epochs 1,000–3,000 (8, 14, 11 failures from it) and had it open at 5,000. So on this house the score at the last epoch moves by about 6 points with the state of one room, whichever arm is trained.
  • Second training seed: no segment 99.6 %, LBS 97.1 % (1 and 7 failed of 240; 1 and 6 of them from the same room). In both seed pairs LBS ends lower, by 4 and 6 queries of 240. That is the same direction twice and small: within one run the count moves by up to 17 queries between saved epochs 1,000 apart. Two pairs do not settle a difference of this size; they do rule out a large loss from the segment loss on this house, and they show no gain from it on this house either.
  • Third training seed: no segment 91.2 %, LBS 90.7 % (21 and 22 failed of 240 on planning seed 0; 14 and 15 of them from the same room). Three pairs, LBS lower each time, by 1.7, 2.5 and 0.6 points: a small cost of the segment loss on this house is the consistent reading, and it is smaller than the movement between saved epochs.

Lakeville: the matched pair

No segment, this benchmark’s code, the same seed and GPU as the LBS run: 97.0 %; LBS 90.8 % (the reused run of the earlier study: 97.9 %). Failed queries of 280 at epochs 1,000 to 5,000 (planning seed 0): no segment 43 / 20 / 9 / 10 / 8, LBS 43 / 20 / 22 / 14 / 27. The two runs are identical through epoch 2,000.

Reading the houses together. Lakeville: −6.2 points for LBS (failed queries after the segment loss starts, LBS / no segment: 22 / 9, 14 / 10, 27 / 8); Allensville −1.7, −2.5, −0.6 points in its seed pairs. Klickitat, taken out of the benchmark on 2026-11-20, went the other way in its matched pair: +5.6 points for LBS. So the matched pairs do not show that the segment loss is harmful on the houses, and they do not show that it helps: with one seed pair per house its effect there is within about ±6 points and of either sign, the same size as the movement between saved epochs of a single run. More seeds per house would be needed to say more; the cause of the Lakeville cost is not tested.

The houses: is lift needed?

The arm without lift is Bellman + segment on ntrl-demo’s own input. On Allensville it solves 98.8 %, above LBS. On Lakeville it ends at 44.9 %, below ntrl-demo itself (72.7 %), which has neither part (LBS: 90.8 %). Two parts that help on every maze make these two houses worse when lift is missing, so this needs a mechanism.

  • The failures are stalls, not walls. Lakeville: 54.6 % of the runs stall and 0.5 % go through a wall. On the mazes the same arm failed through walls.
  • The travel times stop growing with distance. On Lakeville the median of learned over true time is 1.04 / 0.91 / 0.54 / 0.27 / 0.15 / 0.10 at 0–4, 4–8, 8–16, 16–32, 32–64, 64–128 cells; the largest learned time is 0.18 where the true one reaches 1.11. Queries solved by true path length (0.5–2, 2–4, 4–8, 8–16, 16–32, 32–64, 64–128 cells): 100 / 100 / 92 / 22 / 0 / 0 / 0 %. The field is right near the goal and flat beyond, so a far goal gives the planner no slope to follow.
  • ntrl-demo alone and LBS keep the far field. In the farthest bin: Lakeville: ntrl-demo 0.96, LBS 0.89, no lift 0.10. So the flat far field is not a limit of the plain input and not a property of the Bellman term as such: it appears when the Bellman term runs without lift on the larger scene.
  • It is there before the segment loss starts (epoch 2,000), so segment is not the cause. Queries longer than 16 cells solved at epochs 1,000 to 5,000 (planning seed 0): Lakeville 0 / 3 / 2 / 0 / 0 of 120; Allensville 0 / 1 / 21 / 60 / 80 of 80. On Allensville the arm also starts with nothing beyond 16 cells and then builds the far field outward, one distance bin after the other; on Lakeville that build-up does not happen within 5,000 epochs.
  • What differs between the houses is their size in cells and, with it, the weight of the Bellman term, which is set as (0.03 / step radius in box units)² and so grows with the square of the scene size: Allensville 3.8, Lakeville 14.1. Whether that weight is the cause is what the control below tests.
  • Control: ntrl-demo trained by this benchmark’s code on Lakeville (same seed; no Bellman, no segment, no lift) solves 72.7 % and has the far field from the start. Queries longer than 16 cells solved at epochs 1,000 to 5,000: ntrl-demo 37 / 42 / 41 / 45 / 53, no lift 0 / 3 / 2 / 0 / 0 of 120. So with the plain input the Bellman term holds the far field down from the first thousand epochs on; the plain input does not take long to learn it.
  • Control: no lift on Lakeville with the Bellman weight cut to Allensville’s (× 0.27, weight 3.8): 48.9 % solved, 48.6 % stalled; at the full weight 44.9 % and 54.6 %. Queries longer than 16 cells solved at epochs 1,000 to 5,000: 1 / 1 / 1 / 8 / 6 of 120; median learned / true time 0.28. So the size of the Bellman weight is not the cause. What is left is the size of the scene in cells itself (83 against 43): why the Bellman term without lift cannot carry the far field across a scene that large is not tested.

How it was run, and what to keep in mind

  • One training seed per arm (87358). On the 22-cell maze of the pair-lift study the same lift + Bellman recipe moved by 2.5 points between three seeds, and on a 40-cell maze by 10; differences of a few points between arms on one scene are within that.
  • Success during training is planning seed 0 on the test queries with the network of that epoch, every 500 epochs (1,000 on the houses). The bar charts are the final network with planning seeds 0, 1 and 2.
  • The arms share their start. The segment loss switches on at epoch 2,000, so up to there LBS and “no segment” are the same recipe, and so are “no Bellman” and the lift alone. They are not the same numbers: the runs went to two different GPUs, and their curves already differ at epoch 500 by that alone. Read differences of a few points before epoch 2,000 as run-to-run variation.
  • Ground truth in the backup. The Bellman arms read the true speed along each candidate step and the true geometry for the collision check (a clearance table of 32 nodes per cell). The learned-speed variant of the pair-lift page is not used here.
  • Reused runs (Gibson: ntrl-demo, no Bellman, no segment) were trained by the earlier studies’ pipelines with the same loop, data, queries, planner and scorer; their curves during training have fewer points.
  • Training time is what each run took on the GPU it happened to get (RTX 3090 or RTX 5070), one run per GPU.
